claim: A kinematic synergy involving the planar covariation of limb segment motion holds in 54 different animal species (10 birds and 44 mammals).
source: Here, we report that a kinematic synergy involving the planar covariation of limb segment motion holds in 54 different animal species (10 birds and 44 mammals), despite large differences in body size, mass (ranging from 30 g to 4 tonnes), limb configuration, and amplitude of movements.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The body mass of analyzed animals ranged from 30 g to 4 tonnes.
source: Here, we report that a kinematic synergy involving the planar covariation of limb segment motion holds in 54 different animal species (10 birds and 44 mammals), despite large differences in body size, mass (ranging from 30 g to 4 tonnes), limb configuration, and amplitude of movements.
evidence: The abstract states the mass range, which is confirmed by Table 1 showing mouse at 0.03 kg (30 g) and elephant at 4050 kg (approximately 4 tonnes).

claim: The kinematic synergy may represent one neuromechanical principle conserved in evolution to save mechanical energy.
source: This kinematic synergy lies at the interface between the neural command signals output by locomotor pattern generators, the mechanics of the body center of mass and the external environment, and it may represent one neuromechanical principle conserved in evolution to save mechanical energy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed kinematic synergy.

claim: The exchange between gravitational potential energy and forward kinetic energy due to pendulum-like oscillations of the centre of body mass has been shown to apply to walking of several legged animals.
source: With regard to energy saving mechanisms, the exchange between the gravitational potential energy and the forward kinetic energy due to pendulum-like oscillations of the centre of body mass (COM) has been shown to apply to walking of several legged animals (Cavagna et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cavagna et al., 1977.

claim: Four main activity patterns output by spinal motoneurones are common to different mammals and birds.
source: With regard to neuromuscular control, four main activity patterns output by spinal motoneurones have been described that are common to different mammals and birds (Dominici et al., 2011; Wenger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dominici et al., 2011 and Wenger et al., 2016.

claim: The four main activity patterns contribute to limb extension at foot touch-down, body-weight support during stance, limb lift-off, and swing.
source: They contribute to the different phases of gait cycle, that is limb extension at foot touch-down, body-weight support during stance, limb lift-off, and swing (Ting et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ting et al., 2015.

claim: The architecture of the central pattern generators is highly conserved across animal species.
source: Also the architecture of the central pattern generators is highly conserved across animal species (Kiehn, 2016; Grillner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kiehn, 2016 and Grillner, 2018.

claim: The planar law of inter-segmental coordination involves the planar covariation of the temporal changes of the elevation angles of the lower limbs in human locomotion.
source: Based on this approach, one law of inter-segmental coordination has been described in human locomotion, which involves the planar covariation of the temporal changes of the elevation angles of the lower limbs (Borghese et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Borghese et al., 1996.

claim: Limb segment rotations covary so that the three-dimensional trajectory of the elevation angles lies close to a plane.
source: Specifically, limb segment rotations covary so that the three-dimensional (3D) trajectory of the elevation angles lies close to a plane.
evidence: This is a description of the planar covariation law based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The planar covariation in humans is not a trivial consequence of the geometrical and kinematic relationships between different limb segments.
source: Importantly, it has been shown that the planar covariation in humans is not a trivial consequence of the geometrical and kinematic relationships between different limb segments (Ivanenko et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ivanenko et al., 2008.

claim: Newly walking toddlers lack an adult-like limb segment planar covariation.
source: Thus, newly walking toddlers lack an adult-like limb segment planar covariation, and children acquire it with walking experience (Cheron et al., 2001b; Dominici et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cheron et al., 2001b and Dominici et al., 2010.

claim: Children acquire adult-like limb segment planar covariation with walking experience.
source: Thus, newly walking toddlers lack an adult-like limb segment planar covariation, and children acquire it with walking experience (Cheron et al., 2001b; Dominici et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cheron et al., 2001b and Dominici et al., 2010.

claim: Spinal cord injured patients often lack the planar covariation.
source: Also, spinal cord injured patients often lack the planar covariation (Grasso et al., 2004a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grasso et al., 2004a.

claim: A significant correlation has been found between the specific orientation of the plane and the net mechanical power output at the COM at different speeds of walking.
source: In fact, a significant correlation has been found between the specific orientation of the plane, or equivalently the phase shift between the angular motion at the shank and foot, and the net mechanical power output at the COM at different speeds of walking (Bianchi et al., 1998a; Bianchi et al., 1998b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bianchi et al., 1998a and Bianchi et al., 1998b.

claim: A planar law of intersegmental coordination applies to bipedal walking of Japanese macaques.
source: Initial evidence for the application of the planar law beyond the human species comes from the observation of a similar law in bipedal walking of Japanese macaques (Ogihara et al., 2012) and common quails (Ogihara et al., 2014), as well as in quadrupedal walking Rhesus monkeys (Courtine et al., 2005), dogs (Catavitello et al., 2015) and cats (Shen and Poppele, 1995; Lacquaniti et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogihara et al., 2012.

claim: A planar law of intersegmental coordination applies to bipedal walking of common quails.
source: Initial evidence for the application of the planar law beyond the human species comes from the observation of a similar law in bipedal walking of Japanese macaques (Ogihara et al., 2012) and common quails (Ogihara et al., 2014), as well as in quadrupedal walking Rhesus monkeys (Courtine et al., 2005), dogs (Catavitello et al., 2015) and cats (Shen and Poppele, 1995; Lacquaniti et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogihara et al., 2014.

claim: A planar law of intersegmental coordination applies to quadrupedal walking of Rhesus monkeys.
source: Initial evidence for the application of the planar law beyond the human species comes from the observation of a similar law in bipedal walking of Japanese macaques (Ogihara et al., 2012) and common quails (Ogihara et al., 2014), as well as in quadrupedal walking Rhesus monkeys (Courtine et al., 2005), dogs (Catavitello et al., 2015) and cats (Shen and Poppele, 1995; Lacquaniti et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Courtine et al., 2005.

claim: A planar law of intersegmental coordination applies to quadrupedal walking of dogs.
source: Initial evidence for the application of the planar law beyond the human species comes from the observation of a similar law in bipedal walking of Japanese macaques (Ogihara et al., 2012) and common quails (Ogihara et al., 2014), as well as in quadrupedal walking Rhesus monkeys (Courtine et al., 2005), dogs (Catavitello et al., 2015) and cats (Shen and Poppele, 1995; Lacquaniti et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Catavitello et al., 2015.

claim: A planar law of intersegmental coordination applies to quadrupedal walking of cats.
source: Initial evidence for the application of the planar law beyond the human species comes from the observation of a similar law in bipedal walking of Japanese macaques (Ogihara et al., 2012) and common quails (Ogihara et al., 2014), as well as in quadrupedal walking Rhesus monkeys (Courtine et al., 2005), dogs (Catavitello et al., 2015) and cats (Shen and Poppele, 1995; Lacquaniti et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shen and Poppele, 1995 and Lacquaniti et al., 1999.

claim: The height of the hip and limb segment proportions impose very different constraints on the range of angular motion across animals.
source: Thus, the height of the hip (or shoulder) above ground and the limb segment proportions impose very different constraints on the range of angular motion across animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational analysis shown in Figure 1A, which illustrates different permissible combinations of elevation angles for different animals.

claim: Transfer of FL angles to HL angles in the cheetah results in aberrant trunk deformations.
source: For instance, transfer of FL angles to HL angles in the cheetah results in aberrant trunk deformations, while transfer of HL angles of the camel to HL angles of the flamingo fails to predict a realistic hip height of the ipsilateral and contralateral limbs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the computational analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Transfer of HL angles of the camel to HL angles of the flamingo fails to predict a realistic hip height of the ipsilateral and contralateral limbs.
source: For instance, transfer of FL angles to HL angles in the cheetah results in aberrant trunk deformations, while transfer of HL angles of the camel to HL angles of the flamingo fails to predict a realistic hip height of the ipsilateral and contralateral limbs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated by the computational analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The stride duration ranged between 0.3 and 3 s across analyzed animals.
source: The stride duration ranged between 0.3 and 3 s, the longest in the hippopotamus (3 s), and the shortest in the mouse (0.3 s) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The longest stride duration was observed in the hippopotamus (3 s).
source: The stride duration ranged between 0.3 and 3 s, the longest in the hippopotamus (3 s), and the shortest in the mouse (0.3 s) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The shortest stride duration was observed in the mouse (0.3 s).
source: The stride duration ranged between 0.3 and 3 s, the longest in the hippopotamus (3 s), and the shortest in the mouse (0.3 s) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The mean trunk orientation during walking corresponded to the most erect posture in humans (93° relative to the horizontal).
source: The mean trunk orientation during walking corresponded to the most erect posture in humans (93° relative to the horizontal) and gibbons (76°), less vertical posture in birds (~10–45°), and nearly horizontal trunk in quadrupeds (8 ± 7°) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The mean trunk orientation during walking in gibbons was 76° relative to the horizontal.
source: The mean trunk orientation during walking corresponded to the most erect posture in humans (93° relative to the horizontal) and gibbons (76°), less vertical posture in birds (~10–45°), and nearly horizontal trunk in quadrupeds (8 ± 7°) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Birds showed less vertical trunk posture (~10–45°) during walking.
source: The mean trunk orientation during walking corresponded to the most erect posture in humans (93° relative to the horizontal) and gibbons (76°), less vertical posture in birds (~10–45°), and nearly horizontal trunk in quadrupeds (8 ± 7°) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Quadrupeds showed nearly horizontal trunk orientation (8 ± 7°) during walking.
source: The mean trunk orientation during walking corresponded to the most erect posture in humans (93° relative to the horizontal) and gibbons (76°), less vertical posture in birds (~10–45°), and nearly horizontal trunk in quadrupeds (8 ± 7°) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Each limb was on the ground for more than half of the gait cycle in all analyzed animals.
source: Animals were free to move spontaneously at their natural speed and each limb was on the ground for more than a half of the gait cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), as expected for walking gait.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The contacts of hindlimbs with the ground were shorter than those of forelimbs by ~10% of the gait cycle in quadrupeds.
source: On average, the contacts of hindlimbs with the ground were shorter than those of forelimbs by ~10% of the gait cycle in quadrupeds (69 ± 5% for HL and 74 ± 4% for FL, n = 35, p<0.001, paired t-test), as Hildebrand (Hildebrand, 1976) also reported for some animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data and is consistent with previous findings by Hildebrand, 1976.

claim: For mammals, the ROMs of thigh, shank, and foot elevation angles were on average 38 ± 22°, 62 ± 16°, 71 ± 23°, respectively.
source: For mammals, the ROMs of thigh, shank, and foot elevation angles were on average 38 ± 22°, 62 ± 16°, 71 ± 23°, respectively, and for the scapula, upper arm, lower arm and hand they were 29 ± 13°, 50 ± 22°, 75 ± 20°, 96 ± 33°, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: For mammals, the ROMs of scapula, upper arm, lower arm and hand elevation angles were 29 ± 13°, 50 ± 22°, 75 ± 20°, 96 ± 33°, respectively.
source: For mammals, the ROMs of thigh, shank, and foot elevation angles were on average 38 ± 22°, 62 ± 16°, 71 ± 23°, respectively, and for the scapula, upper arm, lower arm and hand they were 29 ± 13°, 50 ± 22°, 75 ± 20°, 96 ± 33°, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ROM of the thigh segment in birds was smaller than in mammals by ~27°.
source: For birds, the ROM of the thigh segment was smaller than in mammals (on average by ~27°, p<0.00001, unpaired t-test), while it was larger for the shank (by ~16°, p=0.001) and it did not differ significantly for the foot (p=0.64) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ROM of the shank segment in birds was larger than in mammals by ~16°.
source: For birds, the ROM of the thigh segment was smaller than in mammals (on average by ~27°, p<0.00001, unpaired t-test), while it was larger for the shank (by ~16°, p=0.001) and it did not differ significantly for the foot (p=0.64) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ROM of the foot segment did not differ significantly between birds and mammals.
source: For birds, the ROM of the thigh segment was smaller than in mammals (on average by ~27°, p<0.00001, unpaired t-test), while it was larger for the shank (by ~16°, p=0.001) and it did not differ significantly for the foot (p=0.64) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The planar covariation law of limb segment motions holds for walking in all recorded animal species.
source: We found that the planar covariation law of limb segment motions holds for walking in all recorded animal species, despite significant differences in body size, limb segment configuration and gait parameters (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The planarity index (PV3) ranged from 0.04% to 5.3% across all limbs and animals.
source: The results showed that the planarity was obeyed by all species (PV3 ranged from 0.04% to 5.3% across all limbs and animals) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The planarity of the anatomical angles trajectories is weaker and more variable than that of elevation angles.
source: Therefore, although also the anatomical angles trajectories tend to be constrained close to one plane, the planar coordination of the elevation angles is stronger and less variable, in agreement with what was previously reported for human walking (Borghese et al., 1996; Barliya et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on the comparison of PCA results for anatomical angles versus elevation angles, and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The width of the gait loop in birds (0.54 ± 0.11) was significantly larger than for HL in mammals (0.26 ± 0.06).
source: The width of the loop in birds (0.54 ± 0.11) was significantly larger than for HL in mammals (0.26 ± 0.06) (p=0.00002, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was a difference between HL and FLlow gait loops in quadrupeds.
source: In addition, there was a difference between HL and FLlow (0.49 ± 0.11) and between HL and FLupp (0.31 ± 0.08) gait loops in quadrupeds (p<0.005, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was a difference between HL and FLupp gait loops in quadrupeds.
source: In addition, there was a difference between HL and FLlow (0.49 ± 0.11) and between HL and FLupp (0.31 ± 0.08) gait loops in quadrupeds (p<0.005, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There were no significant differences between the gait loops of birds and FLlow of mammals.
source: There were no significant differences between the loops of birds and FLlow of mammals (p=0.25).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The orientation of the covariation plane differed across animals due to different phase relationships between elevation angles.
source: While planarity of the 3D loops held for all animals (Figure 3B), the orientation of the covariation plane differed, due to different phase relationships between elevation angles.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the u3 vectors shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a higher u3 dispersion for HL than for FL across animals.
source: Note a higher u3 dispersion for HL (Figure 4A) than for FL (Figure 4B), consistent with the greater variability of u3 components in HL noticed above.
evidence: This claim is supported by the visual representation of u3 vectors in Figure 4.

claim: Birds HL showed a von-Mises Fisher distribution with concentration parameter k = 106.9.
source: In particular, this criterion revealed that the four groups (birds HL, mammals HL, mammals FLupp, mammals FLlow) had concentration parameters significantly different (p<0.0001) and belonged to different distribution, respectively a von-Mises Fisher distribution with concentration parameters k = 106.9, a Kent distribution (girdle-like shape) with k = 5.7, and two other von Mises distribution with k = 20.6, k = 33.7.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the directional data using the empirical shape criterion.

claim: Mammals HL showed a Kent distribution (girdle-like shape) with concentration parameter k = 5.7.
source: In particular, this criterion revealed that the four groups (birds HL, mammals HL, mammals FLupp, mammals FLlow) had concentration parameters significantly different (p<0.0001) and belonged to different distribution, respectively a von-Mises Fisher distribution with concentration parameters k = 106.9, a Kent distribution (girdle-like shape) with k = 5.7, and two other von Mises distribution with k = 20.6, k = 33.7.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the directional data using the empirical shape criterion.

claim: Mammals FLupp showed a von Mises distribution with concentration parameter k = 20.6.
source: In particular, this criterion revealed that the four groups (birds HL, mammals HL, mammals FLupp, mammals FLlow) had concentration parameters significantly different (p<0.0001) and belonged to different distribution, respectively a von-Mises Fisher distribution with concentration parameters k = 106.9, a Kent distribution (girdle-like shape) with k = 5.7, and two other von Mises distribution with k = 20.6, k = 33.7.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the directional data using the empirical shape criterion.

claim: Mammals FLlow showed a von Mises distribution with concentration parameter k = 33.7.
source: In particular, this criterion revealed that the four groups (birds HL, mammals HL, mammals FLupp, mammals FLlow) had concentration parameters significantly different (p<0.0001) and belonged to different distribution, respectively a von-Mises Fisher distribution with concentration parameters k = 106.9, a Kent distribution (girdle-like shape) with k = 5.7, and two other von Mises distribution with k = 20.6, k = 33.7.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the directional data using the empirical shape criterion.

claim: The u3 vectors tended to lay on the plane defined by the mean u1 vector across animals.
source: Furthermore, it is worth noting that the vectors were not dispersed randomly on a sphere, but tended to lay on the plane defined by the mean u1 vector across animals (since u1 was roughly the same; overall, it deviated from the mean u1 by 2.4° [spherical standard error] for HL, by 2.7° for FLupp and by 2.6° for FLlow).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the directional data.

claim: The highest correlation between the rotation of the covariation plane (α-angle) and limb parameters was with Δfoot-shank (r2 = 0.5, p<0.0000001).
source: We found that the values of α-angle were best correlated with the phase shift Δfoot-shank (r2 = 0.5, p<0.0000001, Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For HL, the α-angle was significantly correlated with the ratios Lshank/Lfoot (r2 = 0.45, p<0.00004) and Lthigh/Lfoot (r2 = 0.31, p<0.00004).
source: Other relatively high (r2≥0.3) significant correlations were: for HL, the ratios Lshank/Lfoot and Lthigh/Lfoot (r2 = 0.45 and r2 = 0.31, respectively, p<0.00004) and, for FLupp, ROMs of the upper and lower arms (r2 = 0.40 and r2 = 0.32, respectively, p<0.0002), and the phase shift Δupper arm-scapula (r2 = 0.3, p<0.0003, Figure 5A right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the data.

claim: For FLupp, the α-angle was significantly correlated with ROMs of the upper and lower arms (r2 = 0.40 and r2 = 0.32, respectively, p<0.0002).
source: Other relatively high (r2≥0.3) significant correlations were: for HL, the ratios Lshank/Lfoot and Lthigh/Lfoot (r2 = 0.45 and r2 = 0.31, respectively, p<0.00004) and, for FLupp, ROMs of the upper and lower arms (r2 = 0.40 and r2 = 0.32, respectively, p<0.0002), and the phase shift Δupper arm-scapula (r2 = 0.3, p<0.0003, Figure 5A right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the data.

claim: For FLupp, the α-angle was significantly correlated with the phase shift Δupper arm-scapula (r2 = 0.3, p<0.0003).
source: Other relatively high (r2≥0.3) significant correlations were: for HL, the ratios Lshank/Lfoot and Lthigh/Lfoot (r2 = 0.45 and r2 = 0.31, respectively, p<0.00004) and, for FLupp, ROMs of the upper and lower arms (r2 = 0.40 and r2 = 0.32, respectively, p<0.0002), and the phase shift Δupper arm-scapula (r2 = 0.3, p<0.0003, Figure 5A right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: After controlling for phylogenetic signal, the α-angle remained significantly correlated with Δfoot-shank (r2 = 0.37, p<0.00001).
source: After controlling for a potential phylogenetic signal in the response (and, hence, non-independence of the residuals, see Materials and methods), we found that the α-angle remained significantly correlated with Δfoot-shank (r2 = 0.37, p<0.00001) and Δupper arm-scapula (r2 = 0.31, p<0.00001).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic regression analysis.

claim: After controlling for phylogenetic signal, the α-angle remained significantly correlated with Δupper arm-scapula (r2 = 0.31, p<0.00001).
source: After controlling for a potential phylogenetic signal in the response (and, hence, non-independence of the residuals, see Materials and methods), we found that the α-angle remained significantly correlated with Δfoot-shank (r2 = 0.37, p<0.00001) and Δupper arm-scapula (r2 = 0.31, p<0.00001).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic regression analysis.

claim: The distal segment (hand) of FL was the last to initiate the swing phase in contrast to the distal segment (foot) of HL.
source: For instance, one can notice that the distal segment (hand) of FL was the last to initiate the swing phase in contrast to the distal segment (foot) of HL (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the timing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The correlation between the averaged limb segment elevation angles and those of individual strides was high (on average r = 0.98, range 0.7-1).
source: First, the correlation between the averaged limb segment elevation angles and those of individual strides was high (on average r = 0.98, range 0.7-1, the data for all segments and animals being pooled together), consistent with repeatable kinematic data across steps in animals (Faber et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of inter-stride variability and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The distal segment (hand) of FL always followed the lower arm segment (Δhand-lower arm being positive in all strides).
source: For instance, the distal segment (hand) of FL always followed the lower arm segment (Δhand-lower arm being positive in all strides), in contrast to the distal (foot) segment of HL (Δfoot-shank varied but was generally negative).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the timing of minima across individual strides.

claim: The angular standard deviation of the parameter α across strides was 11° in dogs, 12° in donkeys and 6° in humans.
source: For instance, the angular standard deviation of the parameter α (the angle of rotation of u3) across strides was 11° in dogs, 12° in donkeys and 6° in humans (the strides of all animals for each animal species being pooled together), and across animals it was 6° in dogs (n = 6), and 5° in humans (n = 6), while the differences in α across animal species were much larger (~180°, Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of inter-stride and inter-individual variability.

claim: The angular standard deviation of the parameter α across animals was 6° in dogs and 5° in humans.
source: For instance, the angular standard deviation of the parameter α (the angle of rotation of u3) across strides was 11° in dogs, 12° in donkeys and 6° in humans (the strides of all animals for each animal species being pooled together), and across animals it was 6° in dogs (n = 6), and 5° in humans (n = 6), while the differences in α across animal species were much larger (~180°, Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of inter-individual variability.

claim: The differences in α across animal species were much larger (~180°) than inter-stride or inter-individual variability.
source: For instance, the angular standard deviation of the parameter α (the angle of rotation of u3) across strides was 11° in dogs, 12° in donkeys and 6° in humans (the strides of all animals for each animal species being pooled together), and across animals it was 6° in dogs (n = 6), and 5° in humans (n = 6), while the differences in α across animal species were much larger (~180°, Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of variability within and across species.

claim: The planar law of inter-segmental coordination held in all studied mammals and birds despite significant variations in body size, mass, limb configuration, stride duration and relative amplitude of angular movements.
source: The results showed that, despite significant variations in body size, mass, limb configuration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), stride duration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) and relative amplitude of angular movements (Figure 2), the planar law of inter-segmental coordination held in all studied mammals and birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4), suggesting that this kinematic synergy is ubiquitous in terrestrial locomotion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the comprehensive analysis of 54 species.

claim: The kinematic synergy is ubiquitous in terrestrial locomotion.
source: The results showed that, despite significant variations in body size, mass, limb configuration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), stride duration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) and relative amplitude of angular movements (Figure 2), the planar law of inter-segmental coordination held in all studied mammals and birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4), suggesting that this kinematic synergy is ubiquitous in terrestrial locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that the planar law holds across all 54 studied species.

claim: The planarity index (PV3 ~1–3%) and the orientation of the covariation plane for the bird, human and dog were similar to those reported in previous studies.
source: Even though different recording systems were used in these previous studies, the planarity index (PV3 ~1–3%) and the orientation of the covariation plane (u3 vector) for the bird (Ogihara et al., 2014), human (Bianchi et al., 1998a) and dog (Catavitello et al., 2015) were similar to those reported in the current study (Figure 3), confirming the reliability of our kinematic recordings and suggesting that each animal adopted its own pattern of the inter-segmental coordination.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies and validates the current methodology.

claim: Each animal adopted its own pattern of inter-segmental coordination.
source: Even though different recording systems were used in these previous studies, the planarity index (PV3 ~1–3%) and the orientation of the covariation plane (u3 vector) for the bird (Ogihara et al., 2014), human (Bianchi et al., 1998a) and dog (Catavitello et al., 2015) were similar to those reported in the current study (Figure 3), confirming the reliability of our kinematic recordings and suggesting that each animal adopted its own pattern of the inter-segmental coordination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of species-specific patterns in the orientation of the covariation plane.

claim: In human bipedal walking there is some rotation (although relatively small) of the covariation plane with speed.
source: For instance, in human bipedal walking there is some rotation (although relatively small) of the covariation plane with speed (Bianchi et al., 1998a), while in human crawling the orientation of the covariation plane does not depend on speed (MacLellan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In human crawling the orientation of the covariation plane does not depend on speed.
source: For instance, in human bipedal walking there is some rotation (although relatively small) of the covariation plane with speed (Bianchi et al., 1998a), while in human crawling the orientation of the covariation plane does not depend on speed (MacLellan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacLellan et al., 2017.

claim: Specific limb proportions may play an essential role in the kinematics and energetics of walking.
source: Specific limb proportions may play an essential role in the kinematics and energetics of walking (Leurs et al., 2011), and they have an impact on a locomotor body schema used for controlling step length (Ivanenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Limb proportions have an impact on a locomotor body schema used for controlling step length.
source: Specific limb proportions may play an essential role in the kinematics and energetics of walking (Leurs et al., 2011), and they have an impact on a locomotor body schema used for controlling step length (Ivanenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ivanenko et al., 2011.

claim: In humans elongation of the shank segment relative to the thigh segment affects the amplitude of distal vs. proximal segment oscillations.
source: For instance, in humans elongation of the shank segment relative to the thigh segment (either surgically or using specially designed stilts) affects the amplitude of distal vs. proximal segment oscillations (Dominici et al., 2009) and the optimal step length and walking speed (Leurs et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dominici et al., 2009.

claim: In humans elongation of the shank segment relative to the thigh segment affects the optimal step length and walking speed.
source: For instance, in humans elongation of the shank segment relative to the thigh segment (either surgically or using specially designed stilts) affects the amplitude of distal vs. proximal segment oscillations (Dominici et al., 2009) and the optimal step length and walking speed (Leurs et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leurs et al., 2011.

claim: The Lshank/Lfoot and Lthigh/Lfoot ratios showed 10-fold differences across the sample of animals.
source: For instance, the Lshank/Lfoot and Lthigh/Lfoot ratios showed 10-fold differences in our sample of animals (range 0.5–5).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of limb segment proportions from the experimental data.

claim: The planar covariation holds for animals with very different limb segment configurations.
source: Therefore, it is important to stress that the planar covariation holds for animals with very different limb segment configurations.
evidence: This is an important conclusion based on the finding that planar covariation holds despite 10-fold differences in limb proportions.

claim: The orientation of the covariation plane reflects specific phase relationships in the control of segment motions.
source: While biomechanics contributes to the planar law of inter-segmental coordination (e.g. we found that the u3 vector rotation correlated with Lshank/Lfoot and Lthigh/Lfoot), the orientation of the covariation plane reflects specific phase relationships in the control of segment motions (Bianchi et al., 1998b; Lacquaniti et al., 2002; Ivanenko et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Birds form a group of animals with a compact orientation of the u3 vector close to the thigh axis.
source: For instance, birds form a group of animals with a compact orientation of the u3 vector close to the thigh axis (Figure 4A, see also Ogihara et al., 2014) while primates show rather variable u3 orientation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: Primates show rather variable u3 orientation.
source: For instance, birds form a group of animals with a compact orientation of the u3 vector close to the thigh axis (Figure 4A, see also Ogihara et al., 2014) while primates show rather variable u3 orientation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Birds show characteristically wide gait loops, while for other animals the loops are much narrower for HL.
source: Also, birds show characteristically wide gait loops, while for other animals the loops are much narrower for HL (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: For quadrupedal animals, the orientation of the covariation plane is noticeably different for HL and FL.
source: Finally, for quadrupedal animals, the orientation of the covariation plane is noticeably different for HL and FL (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: HL and FL kinematics are characterized by limb-specific differences in the orientation of the covariation plane.
source: HL and FL kinematics are characterized by limb-specific differences in the orientation of the covariation plane (Figures 3 and 4), the width of the gait loop (the FLlow loop was wider than the HL loop, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and the amplitude (Figure 2) and phase (Figure 5B) of angular motion of distal segments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The FLlow loop was wider than the HL loop.
source: HL and FL kinematics are characterized by limb-specific differences in the orientation of the covariation plane (Figures 3 and 4), the width of the gait loop (the FLlow loop was wider than the HL loop, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and the amplitude (Figure 2) and phase (Figure 5B) of angular motion of distal segments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results confirm previous observations about different orientation of the HL and FL covariation planes in Rhesus monkey.
source: These results confirm previous observations about different orientation of the HL and FL covariation planes in Rhesus monkey (Courtine et al., 2005), dog (Catavitello et al., 2015) and human crawling (MacLellan et al., 2017), and point to the differential control of FL and HL segments in a wide range of mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The results confirm previous observations about different orientation of the HL and FL covariation planes in dog.
source: These results confirm previous observations about different orientation of the HL and FL covariation planes in Rhesus monkey (Courtine et al., 2005), dog (Catavitello et al., 2015) and human crawling (MacLellan et al., 2017), and point to the differential control of FL and HL segments in a wide range of mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Catavitello et al., 2015.

claim: The results confirm previous observations about different orientation of the HL and FL covariation planes in human crawling.
source: These results confirm previous observations about different orientation of the HL and FL covariation planes in Rhesus monkey (Courtine et al., 2005), dog (Catavitello et al., 2015) and human crawling (MacLellan et al., 2017), and point to the differential control of FL and HL segments in a wide range of mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacLellan et al., 2017.

claim: The results point to the differential control of FL and HL segments in a wide range of mammals.
source: These results confirm previous observations about different orientation of the HL and FL covariation planes in Rhesus monkey (Courtine et al., 2005), dog (Catavitello et al., 2015) and human crawling (MacLellan et al., 2017), and point to the differential control of FL and HL segments in a wide range of mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in covariation plane orientation between FL and HL across multiple species.

claim: There are neurophysiological differences in the neurotransmitter systems of FL versus HL spinal locomotor controllers.
source: Finally, neurophysiological differences in the neurotransmitter systems of FL versus HL spinal locomotor controllers (Gerasimenko et al., 2009), a strong asymmetry of projections from spinal controllers on neurons for FL versus HL areas of the motor cortex (Zelenin et al., 2011), and limb-specific features in the organization and coupling between FL and HL spinal controllers (Shik and Orlovsky, 1965; Miller et al., 1975; Yamaguchi, 1986) point to limb-specific organization of central pattern generators, with propriospinal linkages facilitating the coordination between FL and HL (Frigon, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerasimenko et al., 2009.

claim: There is a strong asymmetry of projections from spinal controllers on neurons for FL versus HL areas of the motor cortex.
source: Finally, neurophysiological differences in the neurotransmitter systems of FL versus HL spinal locomotor controllers (Gerasimenko et al., 2009), a strong asymmetry of projections from spinal controllers on neurons for FL versus HL areas of the motor cortex (Zelenin et al., 2011), and limb-specific features in the organization and coupling between FL and HL spinal controllers (Shik and Orlovsky, 1965; Miller et al., 1975; Yamaguchi, 1986) point to limb-specific organization of central pattern generators, with propriospinal linkages facilitating the coordination between FL and HL (Frigon, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zelenin et al., 2011.

claim: There are limb-specific features in the organization and coupling between FL and HL spinal controllers.
source: Finally, neurophysiological differences in the neurotransmitter systems of FL versus HL spinal locomotor controllers (Gerasimenko et al., 2009), a strong asymmetry of projections from spinal controllers on neurons for FL versus HL areas of the motor cortex (Zelenin et al., 2011), and limb-specific features in the organization and coupling between FL and HL spinal controllers (Shik and Orlovsky, 1965; Miller et al., 1975; Yamaguchi, 1986) point to limb-specific organization of central pattern generators, with propriospinal linkages facilitating the coordination between FL and HL (Frigon, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shik and Orlovsky, 1965; Miller et al., 1975; and Yamaguchi, 1986.

claim: Propriospinal linkages facilitate the coordination between FL and HL.
source: Finally, neurophysiological differences in the neurotransmitter systems of FL versus HL spinal locomotor controllers (Gerasimenko et al., 2009), a strong asymmetry of projections from spinal controllers on neurons for FL versus HL areas of the motor cortex (Zelenin et al., 2011), and limb-specific features in the organization and coupling between FL and HL spinal controllers (Shik and Orlovsky, 1965; Miller et al., 1975; Yamaguchi, 1986) point to limb-specific organization of central pattern generators, with propriospinal linkages facilitating the coordination between FL and HL (Frigon, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Frigon, 2017.

claim: The temporal structure of FL and HL muscle activation patterns is limb-specific.
source: The temporal structure of FL and HL muscle activation patterns is limb-specific too, as is the orientation of the covariation plane (e.g. in the dog, Catavitello et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Catavitello et al., 2015.

claim: The orientation of the covariation plane (normal to the plane, u3) varies more for HL than for FL across animals.
source: Furthermore, the orientation of the covariation plane (normal to the plane, u3) varies more for HL than for FL across animals (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Main kinematic adaptations seem to occur in hindlimbs rather than in forelimbs both across animals and across gaits.
source: Thus, main kinematic adaptations seem to occur in hindlimbs rather than in forelimbs both across animals (Figures 4 and 5) and across gaits (Fischer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and previous findings.

claim: There is considerable adaptability or flexibility in the phase relationships of HL segment motion.
source: This implies considerable adaptability or flexibility in the phase relationships of HL segment motion, which will be considered in the following section.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variability in HL covariation plane orientation.

claim: The phylogenetic signal (K index) for the α-angle for HL was statistically significant but rather low (K = 0.10, n = 54, p=0.04).
source: Although the K index (Blomberg et al., 2003, see Materials and methods) we used for the presence of a phylogenetic signal in the α-angle for HL was statistically significant, its value was rather low (K = 0.10, n = 54, p=0.04) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the pattern of α-angles distribution is hardly dependent on phylogenetic relatedness of the species considered.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis of the data.

claim: The pattern of α-angles distribution is hardly dependent on phylogenetic relatedness of the species considered.
source: Although the K index (Blomberg et al., 2003, see Materials and methods) we used for the presence of a phylogenetic signal in the α-angle for HL was statistically significant, its value was rather low (K = 0.10, n = 54, p=0.04) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the pattern of α-angles distribution is hardly dependent on phylogenetic relatedness of the species considered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low phylogenetic signal.

claim: The planar covariation is a feature that has arisen independently several times during evolutionary history.
source: This suggests that the planar covariation is a feature that has arisen independently several times during evolutionary history (Ogihara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the weak phylogenetic signal and is consistent with previous suggestions.

claim: A convergent evolution of this kinematic synergy may be due to both adaptation and constraints acting similarly in distantly related species.
source: A convergent evolution of this kinematic synergy may be due to both adaptation and constraints acting similarly in distantly related species.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the convergent evolution of the kinematic synergy.

claim: Adaptation would arise due to the advantage of a kinematic control law lying at the interface between neural commands and environment.
source: Adaptation would arise due to the advantage of a kinematic control law lying at the interface between neural commands and environment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the adaptive advantage of the kinematic synergy.

claim: Constraints would depend on the inherent biomechanical coupling between different limb segments.
source: Constraints would depend on the inherent biomechanical coupling between different limb segments.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the constraints that may contribute to the kinematic synergy.

claim: The planar covariation law may emerge from the coupling of neural oscillators with limb mechanical oscillators.
source: The planar covariation law may emerge from the coupling of neural oscillators with limb mechanical oscillators (Lacquaniti et al., 2002; Lacquaniti et al., 2012), by adjusting the phase of unit burst generators for each joint, segment or groups of muscles (Grillner, 1981; Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The basic mechanism of rhythmic movements is a phase control of muscle activity.
source: The basic mechanism of rhythmic movements is a phase control of muscle activity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Myoelectric signal analysis demonstrated a burst-like temporal organization of basic muscle activation patterns shared by many animal species.
source: In particular, myoelectric signal analysis demonstrated a burst-like temporal organization of basic muscle activation patterns shared by many animal species (Giszter et al., 2010; Dominici et al., 2011; Lacquaniti et al., 2013), consistent with the existence of a rhythm-generating layer or 'time-keeping function' of the central pattern generator for locomotion (Prentice et al., 1995; McCrea and Rybak, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Muscle activations intervene only during limited time epochs at specific phases of the gait cycle to re-excite the intrinsic oscillations of the system when energy is lost.
source: Because the activation patterns are pulsatile, muscle activations intervene only during limited time epochs at specific phases of the gait cycle to re-excite the intrinsic oscillations of the system when energy is lost (Lacquaniti et al., 1999; Lacquaniti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This represents a fundamental energy-saving principle of control.
source: This represents a fundamental energy-saving principle of control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of pulsatile muscle activation.

claim: The dynamic behavior of the musculo-skeletal system can be modeled through a linear combination of basic muscle patterns, activated sequentially at touch-down, body-weight support, limb lift-off, and swing.
source: The dynamic behavior of the musculo-skeletal system can be modeled through a linear combination of these basic muscle patterns, activated sequentially at touch-down, body-weight support, limb lift-off, and swing (Lacquaniti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The specific orientation of the planar covariation is related to the timing of basic muscle activation patterns.
source: The specific orientation of the planar covariation is related to the timing of basic muscle activation patterns.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: In humans, changes in the orientation of the covariation plane with walking speed are associated with changes in the timing of basic muscle activation patterns.
source: In humans, changes in the orientation of the covariation plane with walking speed (Bianchi et al., 1998b) or across different gaits (Ivanenko et al., 2007) are associated with changes in the timing of basic muscle activation patterns (Ivanenko et al., 2004; Cappellini et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In dogs, the phase-coupling between the elevation angles differs systematically between HL and FL, just as the phase-coupling of the muscle activation patterns.
source: In dogs, the phase-coupling between the elevation angles differs systematically between HL and FL (Figure 4), just as the phase-coupling of the muscle activation patterns (Catavitello et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Central pattern generators may control patterns of limb segment motion rather than patterns of muscle activity.
source: Thus, although it is often assumed that central pattern generators control patterns of muscle activity, an equally plausible hypothesis is that they control patterns of limb segment motion (Lacquaniti et al., 1999; Lacquaniti et al., 2002), since the phase relationships between them are inherently inter-related.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The full limb behavior can be expressed as the two degrees-of-freedom planar motion for each animal, plus the rotation of the plane about a defined axis.
source: The full limb behavior can be expressed as the two degrees-of-freedom planar motion for each animal, plus the rotation of the plane about a defined axis (Figure 4, see also Ivanenko et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a summary of the kinematic description based on the current data and previous work.

claim: The phase shift between foot and shank segments represents an important parametric tuning of the covariation plane rotation to adapt to animal-specific locomotor patterns.
source: Therefore, the phase shift between foot and shank segments represents an important parametric tuning of the covariation plane rotation to adapt to animal-specific locomotor patterns (Figure 4A), walking speed (Bianchi et al., 1998b), gait (Ivanenko et al., 2007) or walking on different support surfaces (Dominici et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: By changing the phase of the foot segment waveform relative to the shank segment from 20° to −50°, the covariation plane rotates similarly to the plane rotation actually observed across animals.
source: Thus, by changing the phase of the foot segment waveform relative to the shank segment from 20° to −50° (corresponding to the same range of Δfoot-shank in Figure 5A), the covariation plane rotates similarly to the plane rotation actually observed across animals (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the harmonic oscillator model shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a similar plane of rotation of the u3 vector across animals and across different human gaits.
source: Note a similar plane of rotation of the u3 vector across animals and across different human gaits.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PC1 mainly reproduces the changes of limb orientation while PC2 is mainly limited to changes in limb length.
source: Examples of stick diagrams generated by such shifts are shown in Figure 6C, demonstrating that PC1 mainly reproduces the changes of limb orientation while PC2 is mainly limited to changes in limb length.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The planar covariation law previously established for humans holds for the terrestrial walk of several mammals and birds.
source: We showed that the planar covariation law previously established for humans holds for the terrestrial walk of several mammals and birds.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: This kinematic synergy lies at the interface between the neural command signals output by central pattern generators and the mechanics of the body COM.
source: This kinematic synergy lies at the interface between two highly conserved phenomena in animal locomotion, the neural command signals output by central pattern generators on the one hand, and the mechanics of the body COM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the kinematic synergy.

claim: The kinematic synergy may represent one specific neuromechanical principle of control of the instantaneous position of the COM, thus contributing to net mechanical energy savings.
source: The kinematic synergy may therefore represent one specific neuromechanical principle of control of the instantaneous position of the COM, thus contributing to net mechanical energy savings.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the kinematic synergy.

claim: The present findings suggest a modular control organization whereby appropriate coordination of the limb segments for each animal can be reduced to two independent components.
source: The present findings suggest a modular control organization whereby appropriate coordination of the limb segments for each animal can be reduced to two independent components.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA results showing that two principal components account for most of the variance.

claim: The orientation of the covariation plane remarkably differed between HL and FL and between animals, especially for HL.
source: The orientation of the covariation plane remarkably differed between HL and FL and between animals, especially for HL (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The major changes in HL plane across animals were associated with the second PC related to the limb length covariation.
source: The major changes in HL plane across animals were associated with the second PC related to the limb length covariation (u2 vector, Figure 6A), probably reflecting different distribution of stiffness and phase control of oscillations and thus the relative rotation of limb segments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of principal components.

claim: Specific limb segment phase relationships are likely advantageous for each individual animal species, and might be the result of evolution.
source: Specific limb segment phase relationships are likely advantageous for each individual animal species, and might be the result of evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the evolutionary significance of species-specific phase relationships.

claim: Birds could adopt a specific yielding kinematic synergy related to their mastery of flight techniques, take-off and landing manoeuvres.
source: For instance, birds master flight techniques, perform take-off and landing manoeuvres, and accordingly they could adopt a specific yielding kinematic synergy (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the specific kinematic synergy observed in birds.

claim: In quadrupeds, different biomechanical functions of HL and FL imply limb-specific couplings of neural oscillators with limb mechanical oscillators.
source: In quadrupeds, different biomechanical functions of HL and FL imply limb-specific couplings of neural oscillators with limb mechanical oscillators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences between HL and FL kinematics.

claim: The study provides an integrative view on the dynamic template of limb segment motion across a wide range of animals.
source: In sum, our study provides an integrative view on the dynamic template of limb segment motion across a wide range of animals and prompts further work to understand functional and evolutionary advantages of specific planar covariation patterns adopted by different species.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: Most recordings involved free walking in a natural environment.
source: Most recordings involved free walking in a natural environment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: For all animals, horizontal limb endpoint excursions were significantly larger than the vertical ones.
source: For all animals, horizontal limb endpoint excursions were significantly larger than the vertical ones, and for some animals they were relatively small (e.g. for artiodactyls) while for others (e.g. for carnivores, empty squares in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F) they exceeded the limb length (1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: For quadrupeds, horizontal limb excursions were significantly greater for FL (0.95L) than for HL (0.87L).
source: In general, for quadrupeds, horizontal limb excursions were significantly greater for FL (0.95L) than for HL (0.87L).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The mean RMS difference between the angular waveforms of the current study and corresponding ones from previous studies was 5.5 ± 3.1°.
source: Thus, on average the root mean square (RMS) difference between the angular waveforms of our study and the corresponding ones of the previous studies was 5.5 ± 3.1°, and the average correlation coefficient between angular waveforms was 0.94 (obtained by pooling all segments and all steps together.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with published data to validate the markerless approach.

claim: The average correlation coefficient between angular waveforms of the current study and previous studies was 0.94.
source: Thus, on average the root mean square (RMS) difference between the angular waveforms of our study and the corresponding ones of the previous studies was 5.5 ± 3.1°, and the average correlation coefficient between angular waveforms was 0.94 (obtained by pooling all segments and all steps together.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with published data to validate the markerless approach.

claim: The angular difference between u3 vectors from the current study and previous studies was on average 0.7° for HL and 0.5° for FLlow.
source: Furthermore, the orientation of the covariation plane derived from both sets of studies was almost identical: the angular difference between u3 vectors was on average 0.7° for HL and 0.5° for FLlow.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with published data to validate the methodology.

claim: The mean RMS difference between the angular waveforms obtained by two different persons was 3 ± 3°.
source: The mean RMS difference between the angular waveforms obtained by the two persons was 3 ± 3° and the mean correlation coefficient was 0.99 (all elevation angles and all strides being pooled together).
evidence: This claim is based on inter-rater reliability analysis.

claim: The mean correlation coefficient between angular waveforms obtained by two different persons was 0.99.
source: The mean RMS difference between the angular waveforms obtained by the two persons was 3 ± 3° and the mean correlation coefficient was 0.99 (all elevation angles and all strides being pooled together).
evidence: This claim is based on inter-rater reliability analysis.

claim: The difference in the orientation of the covariance plane (u3) obtained by two different persons was on average 0.8° for HL, 2.0° for FLupp and 2.5° for FLlow.
source: The corresponding difference in the orientation of the covariance plane (u3) obtained by the two persons was low: on average 0.8° for HL, 2.0° for FLupp and 2.5° for FLlow.
evidence: This claim is based on inter-rater reliability analysis.
